A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: For fixed $u<v$ and Borel $A$, the integrand $1_A(x)p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)$ is nonnegative and jointly Borel in $(y,x)$. Tonelli's parameter-integral clause [F2] makes its integral Borel in $y$; division by the positive Borel function $p_{T-u}(y)$ preserves measurability. For each fixed $y$ the numerator defines a measure in $A$ by countable additivity of the Lebesgue integral.

Taking $A=\mathbb R^d$ in the formula gives $K_{u,v}(y,\mathbb R^d)=p_{T-u}(y)/p_{T-u}(y)=1$ by the marginal identity, so each $K_{u,v}(y,\cdot)$ is a probability measure. The identity kernel at $u=v$ is also a probability kernel.

If $u<v<w$, Tonelli and the two density ratios give $\displaystyle \int K_{v,w}(x,A)K_{u,v}(y,dx)=\frac{\int_A p_{T-w}(z)\int q(T-w,z;T-v,x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)\,dx\,dz}{p_{T-u}(y)}.$ The inner integral is $q(T-w,z;T-u,y)$ by forward Chapman–Kolmogorov, so the expression is $K_{u,w}(y,A)$. If two adjacent times coincide, composition with the identity kernel gives the same equality.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

No path continuity, no right continuity of the filtration, and no completeness
of the underlying probability space is imposed by this definition. Choice
enters only through the conditional-expectation interface named above,
whose countable-choice obligations are declared as dependencies of this item.

Assume AC. Let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $p>1$, and $q=p/(p-1)$. If $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a nonnegative submartingale and $X_N\in L^p$, then
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}X_k\right\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p.$$
In particular, for a martingale $M$ with $M_N\in L^p$,
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}|M_k|\right\|_p\le q\|M_N\|_p.$$

Assume AC. Let $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a filtration, and let $(D_k)_{k\ge1}$ be real square-integrable martingale differences relative to it. For $1\le i<j$, $E[D_iD_j]=0$, so their real $L^2$ inner product is zero. For every $n\ge0$, $E[(\sum_{k=1}^nD_k)^2]=\sum_{k=1}^nE[D_k^2]$.

Assume AC. Let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $p>1$, and $q=p/(p-1)$. If $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a nonnegative submartingale and $X_N\in L^p$, then
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}X_k\right\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p.$$
In particular, for a martingale $M$ with $M_N\in L^p$,
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}|M_k|\right\|_p\le q\|M_N\|_p.$$

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Fix processes $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ and $Y=(Y_t)_{t\ge0}$ of real random
variables on one probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$: for every
$\omega$ in a measurable event of probability one the paths $t\mapsto X_t$
and $t\mapsto Y_t$ are continuous on $[0,\infty)$
[[def-continuity-real]]. Fix $T>0$ and a deterministic partition sequence
$(\pi_n)$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh tending to $0$
[[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]]. For each $n$ write
$\pi_n=(m_n,s^{(n)})$ and form the two families of **cross-increment partial
sums**
$$S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t):=\sum_{\substack{1\le k\le m_n\\s^{(n)}_k\le t}}\bigl(X_{s^{(n)}_k}-X_{s^{(n)}_{k-1}}\bigr)\bigl(Y_{s^{(n)}_k}-Y_{s^{(n)}_{k-1}}\bigr),$$
$$S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(t):=S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t)+\bigl(X_t-X_{s^{(n)}_{k(t)}}\bigr)\bigl(Y_t-Y_{s^{(n)}_{k(t)}}\bigr)\quad(k(t)<m_n),$$
with $S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(T):=S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(T)$ and $k(t)$ the largest
index in $\{0,\ldots,m_n\}$ with $s^{(n)}_{k(t)}\le t$; these are the cross sums corresponding to the
two conventions of
[[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]] specialized to the pair
$(X,Y)$, and both are $0$ at $t=0$.

All suprema in probability statements below use measurable versions. For
any finite collection of the processes involved, including a candidate limit,
intersect their measurable probability-one continuity events and set all of
them to zero off that intersection. These representatives have everywhere
continuous paths and retain measurable fixed-time values. The partial-sum
paths are continuous; the step-sum paths are right-continuous on $[0,T)$
with the specified value at $T$. Their uniform distances from a continuous
candidate therefore equal suprema over $(\mathbb Q\cap[0,T])\cup\{T\}$,
which are finite measurable random variables. Another such normalization
agrees on a measurable probability-one event and gives the same probability
limits. Here indistinguishability means agreement at every time on a
measurable probability-one event. No completeness or adaptedness is needed
for this convention.

1. **Existence and value of the covariation.** We say that the **quadratic
   covariation $[X,Y]$ exists on $[0,T]$** when there is a real process
   $t\mapsto[X,Y]_t$ of real random variables with almost-sure continuous
   paths on $[0,T]$ such that for *every* deterministic partition
   sequence $(\pi_n)$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh tending to $0$ both families
   converge to it uniformly in probability on $[0,T]$:
   $$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\bigl|S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t)-[X,Y]_t\bigr|\longrightarrow0, \qquad \sup_{0\le t\le T}\bigl|S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(t)-[X,Y]_t\bigr|\longrightarrow0,$$
   the convergence being convergence in probability
   [[def-convergence-in-probability]]. The two displayed requirements are part
   of one condition: the same process $[X,Y]$ must arise for every admissible
   sequence and for both conventions. When the condition holds we call
   $[X,Y]_t$ the **quadratic covariation of $X$ and $Y$ at time $t$**, and we
   write $[X]:=[X,X]$ and call it the **quadratic variation of $X$**. For two candidate limits $U,V$, fix a deterministic dyadic partition
   sequence. The triangle inequality bounds $\sup_t|U_t-V_t|$ by the sum
   of their uniform errors against its partial sums. For each
   $\varepsilon>0$ the probability that this supremum exceeds
   $\varepsilon$ is at most the sum of the two error probabilities at
   $\varepsilon/2$, and hence is zero. Taking $\varepsilon=1/j$,
   $j\ge1$, proves uniqueness on one measurable probability-one event; the definition is applied
   separately on each finite horizon, and when the covariations on all
   horizons are compatible we write the resulting process on $[0,\infty)$
   again as $[X,Y]$.

2. **Symmetry and polarization.** Exchanging the two factors does not change
   the definition, so $[X,Y]=[Y,X]$ whenever either side exists. The
   identities
   $$[X+Y]=[X]+2[X,Y]+[Y],\qquad [X-Y]=[X]-2[X,Y]+[Y]$$
   hold on the domain where all covariations appearing in them exist: the
   cross-increment sums are bilinear in the pair, so the displayed identities
   are exact at the level of partial sums for every partition, and probability
   limits pass through finite algebraic identities. In particular
   $[X,Y]=\tfrac12\bigl([X+Y]-[X]-[Y]\bigr)$ and
   $4[X,Y]=[X+Y]-[X-Y]$ on that domain.

3. **Bilinearity and insensitivity to constants.** If the covariations
   $[X_1,Y]$, $[X_2,Y]$ and $[X_1+X_2,Y]$ exist on $[0,T]$, then
   $[X_1+X_2,Y]=[X_1,Y]+[X_2,Y]$ there, and $[cX,Y]=c[X,Y]$ for real $c$;
   moreover $[X+c,Y]=[X,Y]$ for every real constant $c$, because the
   increments of a constant process are zero. These are again exact
   identities of partial sums plus uniqueness of limits.

4. **Zero covariation with a continuous finite-variation process.** Let
   $A=(A_t)$ be continuous on a full-measure event and suppose, for every
   $\omega$ in that event, that $t\mapsto A_t(\omega)$ has bounded variation
   on every finite interval in the sense of
   [[def-bounded-variation-and-total-variation]]. Then for
   each $T$ and each admissible partition sequence, the cross sums of $A$
   against any continuous process $Y$ satisfy
   $$\Bigl|\sum_k\bigl(A_{s_k}-A_{s_{k-1}}\bigr)\bigl(Y_{s_k}-Y_{s_{k-1}}\bigr)\Bigr| \le\Bigl(\max_k\sup_{u,v\in[s_{k-1},s_k]}|Y_u-Y_v|\Bigr)\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(A),$$
   because every sum of absolute $A$-increments is bounded by the path's total
   variation on $[0,T]$; the
   maximum tends to $0$ along vanishing meshes by uniform continuity of the
   continuous path $Y$ on the compact interval $[0,T]$. Hence $[A,Y]$ exists
   and equals the zero process for every such $A$ and every continuous $Y$,
   and in particular $[A,A']=0$ for two such processes. In the notation of the
   page this says that **continuous finite-variation parts contribute nothing
   to quadratic covariation**.

5. **Scope and choice.** The inputs and candidate limits have measurable
   fixed-time values and almost-sure continuous paths. The normalization above
   makes the uniform errors real random variables, as required by
   [[def-convergence-in-probability]]. No filtration or adaptedness is used.
   The algebra in clauses 2--3 passes to limits by the uniform triangle
   inequality and the union bound. In clause 4 the same estimate holds for
   every partial sum, including its terminal partial increment, because its
   intervals are disjoint; it thus proves uniform convergence to zero on the
   common continuity event. For each epsilon, the measurable events that some
   error after index n exceeds epsilon decrease to a null event; continuity
   from above of probability gives convergence in probability. Uniform
   continuity is justified by the choice-free finite-cover argument in
   [[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]]. The partitions are
   given and normalization uses a finite intersection of supplied full-measure
   events, so no choice axiom is used. Existence for Brownian Ito processes is
   a separate theorem, not a presupposition of this definition.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale and $\sigma\le\tau$ are stopping times bounded by a deterministic $N$, then
$$\mathbb E[M_\tau\mid\mathcal F_\sigma]=M_\sigma\quad\text{a.s.},$$
so $\mathbb EM_\tau=\mathbb EM_\sigma$. For a submartingale $X$ the conditional and expectation inequalities point upward; for a supermartingale they point downward.

derivations.claim: If $Q$ is a true continuous martingale and $\rho\le T$ is a stopping time, round $\rho$ up to finite-valued grid stopping times $\rho_m\downarrow\rho$. For fixed $s\le t$, include $s,t$ in the grid; the sampled process is a discrete martingale, so [F5] gives the event-integral identity for $Q_{t\wedge\rho_m}$ and $Q_{s\wedge\rho_m}$. The finite-valued stopping calculation identifies these stopped values as conditional expectations of $Q_T$. They are uniformly integrable: for any sub-$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal H$, truncating $Q_T$ at $K/2$ gives $E(|E[Q_T\mid\mathcal H]|1_{|E[Q_T\mid\mathcal H]|>K})\le2E(|Q_T|1_{|Q_T|>K/2})$. Continuity gives almost-sure convergence as $m\to\infty$; dominated convergence on bounded truncations and this uniform tail bound pass the event identities to $Q^\rho$. Thus a bounded stop of a true continuous martingale is a true martingale. If $M$ is a local martingale with localizers $\lambda_k$, then $M^{\tau\wedge\lambda_k}=(M^{\lambda_k})^\tau$ is a true martingale by this fact, so $(\lambda_k)$ also localizes $M^\tau$. For each integer $n\ge1$, let $\tau_n=\inf\{t\le T:|M_t|\ge n\}\wedge T$ and set $M^{(n)}=M^{\tau_n}$. The stopping-time definition and continuity make $\tau_n$ a stopping time, and the preceding argument shows $M^{(n)}$ is a local martingale. It is bounded by $n$, hence a true martingale: pass its event-integral identities along its localizing sequence by dominated convergence. Every continuous path is bounded on $[0,T]$, so $\tau_n=T$ eventually on each path. It suffices to construct the claimed limit for each bounded martingale $M^{(n)}$ and show the constructions agree on overlaps.

Fix one such bounded martingale $M$, with $|M_t|\le n$, and a deterministic partition $\pi=(t_0,\ldots,t_N)$ of $[0,T]$. Put $H^\pi_s=M_{t_k}$ for $t_k<s\le t_{k+1}$ and $\displaystyle I^\pi_t=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}M_{t_k}\bigl(M_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-M_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr),\qquad Q^\pi_t=\sum_{t_{k+1}\le t}(M_{t_{k+1}}-M_{t_k})^2+(M_t-M_{t_k})^2$ when $t_k\le t<t_{k+1}$, with the last partial term omitted at $t=T$. The process $I^\pi$ is a continuous martingale because it is a finite sum of bounded, left-measurable multiples of martingale increments. Orthogonality [F1] gives $E|I^\pi_T|^2=\sum_kE[M_{t_k}^2(\Delta_kM)^2]\le n^2 E(M_T-M_0)^2\le n^4$. Directly expanding each square yields the exact identity $M_t^2-M_0^2=2I^\pi_t+Q^\pi_t$. Hence $\|Q^\pi_T\|_2\le3n^2$, uniformly over all partitions.

For two partitions $\pi,\rho$, take their common refinement $\eta$. Refinement does not change a step sum with a fixed coefficient on each coarse interval, so $\displaystyle E|I^\pi_T-I^\rho_T|^2=E\sum_{[s,t]\in\eta}(H^\pi_s-H^\rho_s)^2(M_t-M_s)^2\le E\left[R_{\pi,\rho}^2Q^\eta_T\right],$ where $R_{\pi,\rho}=\sup_s|H^\pi_s-H^\rho_s|$. Uniform continuity [F3] gives $R_{\pi,\rho}\to0$ almost surely as both meshes tend to zero, and $R_{\pi,\rho}\le2n$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] and dominated convergence [F2] therefore make the last expectation tend to zero, using the uniform $L^2$ bound on $Q^\eta_T$ from step 1.2. Thus the terminal sums $I^\pi_T$ are Cauchy in $L^2$; completeness [F2] gives their $L^2$ limit, and Doob's inequality [F2] gives the same Cauchy property for $\sup_{t\le T}|I^\pi_t-I^\rho_t|$; for the continuous-time supremum, apply the discrete inequality on increasing finite rational grids and pass to their union by monotone convergence [F2]. Choose a subsequence whose successive expected squared sup errors are at most $2^{-4k}$. Markov's inequality and the union bound imply that this subsequence converges uniformly almost surely to a continuous process $I$; the full family converges uniformly in probability to $I$. For fixed subsequence index $m$, the squared path-sup errors from its $m$th term to later terms converge almost surely to $\sup_{t\le T}|I^{\pi_{n_m}}_t-I_t|^2$. Applying monotone convergence to the infima of these tails gives Fatou's inequality; the $L^2$-Cauchy bound then shows these errors tend to zero in $L^2$. The event-integral martingale identities therefore pass to the $L^1$ limit.

The exact identity in step 1.2 shows that the partial-increment sums $Q^\pi$ converge uniformly in probability to $Q_t=M_t^2-M_0^2-2I_t$. $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let
$M=(M^1,\dots,M^d)$ be an adapted $\mathbb R^d$-valued process with continuous
paths such that every coordinate $M^i$ is a real continuous local martingale
relative to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]. Suppose $M_0=0$ almost surely and
whose quadratic covariations in the sense of
[[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]] satisfy
$[M^i,M^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$ for all $i,j$ and all $t\ge0$. Then $M$ is a
standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]],
and for all $0\le s<t$ the vector increment $M_t-M_s$ is independent of
$\mathcal F_s$ with law $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$, and let $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a real process
that satisfies $X_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$, and has
continuous paths, in the strong sense that $s\mapsto X_s(\omega)$ is continuous
on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$. Then $X$ is progressively
measurable and predictable relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], including at time
zero under the generator convention $\{0\}\times A$, $A\in\mathcal F_0$. No
choice principle is used. Here a filtration means an increasing family of
sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$. The fixed-time measurability hypothesis
is the adaptedness terminology of clause 1 of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]; only that clause is
used, not its conditional-expectation or martingale interface and its Choice
assumption.

If instead the paths are continuous only on an event $A\in\mathcal F$ with
$P(A)=1$, the conclusion holds for the modification that is set equal to $0$
off $A$ provided $A\in\mathcal F_0$; without such a measurability assumption on
the continuity event no predictability claim is made, because predictability
is a property of the given joint map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Assume AC. Let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $p>1$, and $q=p/(p-1)$. If $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a nonnegative submartingale and $X_N\in L^p$, then
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}X_k\right\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p.$$
In particular, for a martingale $M$ with $M_N\in L^p$,
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}|M_k|\right\|_p\le q\|M_N\|_p.$$

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Let $M$ be a real continuous local martingale on $[0,T]$ with $M_0=0$, where a local martingale means that some increasing stopping times tending to $T$ make the stopped processes martingales. 1. A standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion exists: one may take $d$

   assemble them coordinatewise.
2. If $B$ is any standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion and $c>0$, then
   $$Y_t=c^{-1/2}B_{ct},\qquad t\ge0,$$

   elements $B$ and $Y$ have the same law on $(\mathbb R^d)^{[0,\infty)}$
   equipped with its cylinder sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$

3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the

[[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]].
All coefficient path integrals below use zero outside the common measurable

On this event, Cauchy–Schwarz makes every product

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]];
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

$[0,T]$. All cited stochastic-calculus interfaces are used on this interval.
Their constructions require no extension of $W$ beyond $T$: elementary
integrals use only increments between partition points in $[0,T]$, and their
$L^2$ limits and continuous versions are constructed on that same interval.

integrals agree up to the smaller stop by the finite-energy stopping identity.
On the full event of finite energy, $\rho_n=T$ for all sufficiently large

exactly as in the localized construction of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. At $T=0$ every integral is zero.

2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments

$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$

locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In

$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

$$dX^i_t=b^i_t\,dt+\sum_{k=1}^m\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in the closed ball $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, take $X_0$ with law $\mu$, measurable at time zero and independent of the future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for every $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the strong solution of $dX_t=g(t)\,dW_t$ with initial value $X_0$. For $a>0$ define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$, define

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x).$$

Then $p_t$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density of the law of $X_t$. For each $x$, $q(s,x;t,\cdot)$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density, and for all Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$P(X_s\in A,\ X_t\in B)=\int_A\int_B q(s,x;t,y)\,dy\,\mu_s(dx),\qquad \mu_s:=\operatorname{Law}(X_s).$$

For $0\le s<r<t\le T$, these transition densities satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz=q(s,x;t,y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$

No Lebesgue density for the initial law $\mu$ is assumed.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Define $K_{u,v}$ by the Bayes-reversed kernel formula for $0\le u\le v\le T$. Then the reversed process $Y_u=X_{T-u}$ is Markov with transitions $K_{u,v}$, and for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ and $0\le u<T$ its generator is
$$\widetilde L_u\phi(y)=\frac{L_{T-u}^*(p_{T-u}\phi)(y)-\phi(y)L_{T-u}^*p_{T-u}(y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}.$$
Define the natural reversed filtration by $\mathcal G_u=\sigma(Y_r:0\le r\le u)$. The compensated test process is a local martingale relative to $(\mathcal G_u)$, so $Y$ solves the corresponding local martingale problem. Expanding the adjoint product rule gives
$$\widetilde L_u\phi=\widetilde b_u\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12a_{T-u}:D^2\phi,\qquad \widetilde b_u=-b_{T-u}+\nabla\!\cdot a_{T-u}+a_{T-u}\nabla\log p_{T-u},$$
with $(\nabla\!\cdot a)_i=\sum_j\partial_j a_{ij}$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a real continuous local martingale on $[0,T]$ with $M_0=0$, where a local martingale means that some increasing stopping times tending to $T$ make the stopped processes martingales. Then there is a unique continuous increasing process $[M]$ with $[M]_0=0$ such that the step-endpoint and partial-increment sums of squared increments along every deterministic partition sequence whose mesh tends to zero converge uniformly in probability to $[M]$. Moreover $M_t^2-[M]_t$ is a continuous local martingale. For a continuous $d$-dimensional local martingale $M$ started at zero, polarization defines continuous covariations $[M^i,M^j]$ with $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$ local martingales. More generally, if $X=M+A$ and $Z=N+C$ with continuous local martingales $M,N$ and continuous finite-variation processes $A,C$, then left-step sums define the localized integrals against $M,N$ and
$$X_tZ_t-X_0Z_0=\int_0^t X_s\,dZ_s+\int_0^t Z_s\,dX_s+[M,N]_t,$$
where finite-variation integrals are pathwise Lebesgue–Stieltjes integrals and local-martingale integrals are the limits of the displayed left-step sums. Stopping a continuous local martingale at a bounded stopping time preserves its local-martingale property; if the stopped process is bounded, it is a true martingale. A continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$. Let $M$ be a continuous adapted $d$-dimensional local martingale with $M_0=0$. Let $\sigma$ be a predictable process of invertible $d\times d$ matrices, with $\|\sigma_t^{-1}\|\le C$ for a finite deterministic constant $C$ and $\int_0^T\|\sigma_t\|_F^2dt<\infty$ almost surely. Suppose
$$[M^i,M^j]_t=\int_0^t(\sigma_s\sigma_s^{\mathsf T})_{ij}ds.$$
Then predictable elementary sums, completed in the localized bracket-energy norm, define $B=\int\sigma^{-1}dM$. It has an adapted continuous version, is standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion in the given filtration, and
$$M_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$$
up to indistinguishability. The integral on the right is the localized predictable Brownian integral defined by elementary sums and their $L^2$ completion. Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

derivations.claim: For $u<v$, the joint density of $(X_{T-v},X_{T-u})$ is $p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)$. Dividing by the strictly positive later marginal $p_{T-u}(y)$ gives the conditional law of $X_{T-v}$ given $X_{T-u}=y$, exactly $K_{u,v}(y,dx)$. Its normalization and reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov identity follow from [F1], so $Y$ is Markov with those transitions.

Apply [F2] to the Bayes kernels. It gives, for every compactly supported smooth $\phi$, the reverse generator $\displaystyle \widetilde L_u\phi(y)=p_{T-u}(y)^{-1}\{L_{T-u}^*(p_{T-u}\phi)(y)-\phi(y)L_{T-u}^*p_{T-u}(y)\}$ and the corresponding compensated local martingale.

Fix $R$ and stop when $|Y|$ first reaches $R$. Compactly supported cutoffs equal to $x_i$ and $x_ix_j$ on the ball of radius $R$ turn the compact-test martingale identities into coordinate and coordinate-product identities. Subtracting the finite-variation drift in each coordinate identity gives continuous local martingales $M^i$. The product formula in [F4] shows that $Y_iY_j-Y_i(0)Y_j(0)-\int_0^{\cdot}(\widetilde b_iY_j+\widetilde b_jY_i)dr-[M_i,M_j]$ is a local martingale. The coordinate-product test shows that the same expression with $\int_0^{\cdot}a_{ij}(T-r,Y_r)dr$ in place of $[M_i,M_j]$ is a local martingale. Their difference is a continuous finite-variation local martingale, hence constant by [F4]; it starts at zero. Thus $[M_i,M_j]_u=\int_0^u a_{ij}(T-r,Y_r)dr$. Letting $R\uparrow\infty$ is valid because the assumed solution is nonexplosive.

To handle the Borel coefficients allowed by the SDE data, choose the predictable representative $\widehat Y$ obtained as follows: take left-step approximations with coefficients $Y_{kT/2^n}$, set their time-zero value to $Y_0$, and take their pointwise limit where finite and $0$ otherwise. These maps are predictable by [F6] and agree with $Y$ at every time on its common continuity event. The pair $(r,\widehat Y_r)$ is predictable, so the joint Borel coefficient gives a predictable matrix $\Sigma_r=\sigma_{T-r}(\widehat Y_r)$; inversion is Borel on invertible matrices, and $\|\Sigma_r^{-1}\|$ is uniformly bounded. Step 3.2 gives $\int_0^T\|\Sigma_r\|_F^2dr=\operatorname{tr}[M]_T<\infty$ almost surely, as well as $[M]_u=\int_0^u\Sigma_r\Sigma_r^{\mathsf T}dr$. Thus [F5] constructs $B=\int\Sigma^{-1}dM$ Brownian in the original reversed filtration, and proves $M=\int\Sigma\,dB$. Since $\widehat Y=Y$ on a common full event, this is the displayed reverse SDE with its original Borel coefficient. The assumed well-posedness and nonexplosion of the reverse martingale problem identify its law uniquely and complete the theorem.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in the closed ball $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, take $X_0$ with law $\mu$, measurable at time zero and independent of the future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for every $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the strong solution of $dX_t=g(t)\,dW_t$ with initial value $X_0$. For $a>0$ define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$, define

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x).$$

Then $p_t$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density of the law of $X_t$. For each $x$, $q(s,x;t,\cdot)$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density, and for all Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$P(X_s\in A,\ X_t\in B)=\int_A\int_B q(s,x;t,y)\,dy\,\mu_s(dx),\qquad \mu_s:=\operatorname{Law}(X_s).$$

For $0\le s<r<t\le T$, these transition densities satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz=q(s,x;t,y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$

No Lebesgue density for the initial law $\mu$ is assumed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, a finite $R\ge0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ for every $s<t$, and let $X$ be the unique strong solution of $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$. For $a>0$ define $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ set

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),$$

and set $\mu_0=\mu$. Let $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ denote the real infinitely differentiable functions with compact support. For every $t>0$, $p_t$ is positive and infinitely differentiable in $x$. On each interval $[\epsilon,T]$ with $0<\epsilon<T$, it is continuously differentiable in time and satisfies

$$\partial_t p_t(x)=\frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_xp_t(x),\qquad \Delta_x=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2.$$

A family $(\nu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ of Borel probability measures is narrowly continuous when $t\mapsto\int f\,d\nu_t$ is continuous for every bounded continuous real function $f$. It is a weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$ when it is narrowly continuous, $\nu_0=\mu$, and, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and every real-valued function $\psi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first time derivative and continuous spatial derivatives through order two, whose spatial support lies in one compact set for all $s$, it satisfies

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(t,x)\,\nu_t(dx)-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(0,x)\,\mu(dx)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}\left(\partial_s\psi(s,x)+\frac{g(s)^2}{2}\Delta_x\psi(s,x)\right)\nu_s(dx)\,ds.$$

Set $K_{u,u}(y,\cdot)=\delta_y$. These are the Bayes-reversed kernels of the additive Gaussian smoothing process, including the posterior kernel at the original data time; no density for $\mu$ is required.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a real continuous local martingale on $[0,T]$ with $M_0=0$, where a local martingale means that some increasing stopping times tending to $T$ make the stopped processes martingales. Then there is a unique continuous increasing process $[M]$ with $[M]_0=0$ such that the step-endpoint and partial-increment sums of squared increments along every deterministic partition sequence whose mesh tends to zero converge uniformly in probability to $[M]$. Moreover $M_t^2-[M]_t$ is a continuous local martingale. For a continuous $d$-dimensional local martingale $M$ started at zero, polarization defines continuous covariations $[M^i,M^j]$ with $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$ local martingales. More generally, if $X=M+A$ and $Z=N+C$ with continuous local martingales $M,N$ and continuous finite-variation processes $A,C$, then left-step sums define the localized integrals against $M,N$ and
$$X_tZ_t-X_0Z_0=\int_0^t X_s\,dZ_s+\int_0^t Z_s\,dX_s+[M,N]_t,$$
where finite-variation integrals are pathwise Lebesgue–Stieltjes integrals and local-martingale integrals are the limits of the displayed left-step sums. Stopping a continuous local martingale at a bounded stopping time preserves its local-martingale property; if the stopped process is bounded, it is a true martingale. A continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a continuous adapted $d$-dimensional local martingale with $M_0=0$. Let $(\sigma_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a continuous adapted process of invertible $d\times d$ matrices such that $\|\sigma_t^{-1}\|\le C$ for a deterministic finite constant $C$, and suppose every entry of $\sigma$ is locally square-integrable in time almost surely. Write $[M^i,M^j]$ for the continuous bracket characterized by the local-martingale property of $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$, and assume
$$[M^i,M^j]_t=\int_0^t(\sigma_s\sigma_s^{\mathsf T})_{ij}\,ds\qquad(1\le i,j\le d).$$
Then the stochastic integral $B_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s^{-1}\,dM_s$, constructed as the localized $L^2$ limit of left-step sums, has a continuous version with $[B^i,B^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$. Consequently $B$ is a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to the given filtration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable and satisfy $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$; set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces

right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.

$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the

$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable

in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong

integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.

[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,

Brownian motion here means the finite-horizon version of the cited definition:

integrals use only increments between partition points in $[0,T]$, and their

The stopped integrands have expected energy at most $n$; their continuous

[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. At $T=0$ every integral is zero.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $X_t$ have continuous paths on $[0,T]$ and be Markov on $\mathbb R^d$, meaning its conditional future law given the past depends only on its current state; nonexplosive means it remains in $\mathbb R^d$ throughout this finite interval. Let it have forward generator
$$L_t\phi=b_t\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12a_t:D^2\phi,$$
where $a_t=\sigma_t\sigma_t^{\mathsf T}$ is symmetric and $L_t^*r=-\partial_i(b_{t,i}r)+\tfrac12\partial_i\partial_j(a_{t,ij}r)$. Assume positive $C^{1,2}$ marginal densities $p_t$ and positive transition densities $q(s,x;t,y)$ satisfy the marginal identity and Chapman–Kolmogorov identity, and that $\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t$ and $\partial_tq(s,x;t,y)=L_t^{*,y}q(s,x;t,y)$ hold classically. Assume for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ that the transition-density integrals can be differentiated in time, the resulting derivatives are integrable, and integration by parts in the state variable has no boundary term. Define $K_{u,v}$ by the Bayes-reversed kernel formula for $0\le u\le v\le T$. Then the reversed process $Y_u=X_{T-u}$ is Markov with transitions $K_{u,v}$, and for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ and $0\le u<T$ its generator is
$$\widetilde L_u\phi(y)=\frac{L_{T-u}^*(p_{T-u}\phi)(y)-\phi(y)L_{T-u}^*p_{T-u}(y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}.$$
It solves the corresponding local martingale problem. Expanding the adjoint product rule gives
$$\widetilde L_u\phi=\widetilde b_u\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12a_{T-u}:D^2\phi,\qquad \widetilde b_u=-b_{T-u}+\nabla\!\cdot a_{T-u}+a_{T-u}\nabla\log p_{T-u},$$
with $(\nabla\!\cdot a)_i=\sum_j\partial_j a_{ij}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]];
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

Brownian motion here means the finite-horizon version of the cited definition:
$W_0=0$ almost surely, with continuous paths and the stated increments on
$[0,T]$. All cited stochastic-calculus interfaces are used on this interval.
Their constructions require no extension of $W$ beyond $T$: elementary
integrals use only increments between partition points in $[0,T]$, and their
$L^2$ limits and continuous versions are constructed on that same interval.
For a predictable scalar integrand $H$ with finite pathwise energy, localize
at $\rho_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:\int_0^t H_s^2ds\ge n\}\wedge T$.
Here $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$.
The stopped integrands have expected energy at most $n$; their continuous
integrals agree up to the smaller stop by the finite-energy stopping identity.
On the full event of finite energy, $\rho_n=T$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, so these integrals paste uniquely on the whole closed interval $[0,T]$,
exactly as in the localized construction of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. At $T=0$ every integral is zero.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
